# 3-minute pitch script for `walkthrough/index.html`

One row per step of the walkthrough, in order. **Say** is spoken while the step's clip plays (or while the slide is up). **Click** is the highlighted control that ends the step; where it says **→**, press the arrow key (no hotspot on that step). Times are cumulative and assume a calm pace of about 140 words a minute.

Tips: let each clip finish before you click (the blue box appears when it is done). If you fall behind, press → during a clip to jump to its end. The bold words are the ones to land.

---

## Opening

| # | Time | On screen | Say | Click |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0:00–0:10 | Title: "From thousands of customer voices to requirements a PM can defend." | Every new BMW starts with one question: **what should the next one be?** The answers are buried in thousands of customer voices. Let us show you how a product manager turns them into decisions. | **Start the demo** |

## Demo 1: what the challenge asked for

| # | Time | On screen | Say | Click |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2 | 0:10–0:18 | The cursor fills in the product context | First, the PM sets the frame: **5 Series, United States**, 18 months, a team of 12, and the deadline matters a lot. | **Add evidence** |
| 3 | 0:18–0:26 | Evidence panel; a customer-feedback CSV is dropped in | Then we add **our own evidence**: customer comments, market data, trends, even past decisions. Here, a file of customer feedback. | **Preview rows** |
| 4 | 0:26–0:31 | Preview table, features matched | Nothing counts until it is checked. **Every comment is matched to a feature**, and the PM can correct it. | **Add 8 rows** |
| 5 | 0:31–0:34 | "Generate the requirements" | Now, generate. | **Generate requirements** |
| 6 | 0:34–0:45 | Ranked requirements; the cursor opens Interior & Comfort | In seconds, **4,365 real customer findings** become a ranked list, per area of the car. In Interior & Comfort, **seat comfort is number two**. Why? | **Evidence & reasoning** |
| 7 | 0:45–0:55 | The reasoning opens and zooms in | No black box. **88 customers** raised it. And this bar shows **exactly what the score is made of**: customer demand, timeline, market evidence, competitor data. | **View cited sources** |
| 8 | 0:55–1:03 | The sources scroll to Competitors, zoomed | And every number has a source, competitors included: **nine signals** from Mercedes and Audi, each linked to the original. | **→** |
| 9 | 1:03–1:07 | Back to the reasoning | But the AI only proposes. **The PM decides.** | **Move up** |
| 10 | 1:07–1:12 | Seat comfort moves to #1 | Seats matter more than audio settings, so seat comfort goes to **number one**. | **Approve** |
| 11 | 1:12–1:24 | Dictation: the reason appears word by word | And I say why, out loud. **One sentence**, transcribed and saved with the decision. *(let the words finish)* | **Approve requirement** |
| 12 | 1:24–1:29 | The card shows Approved | Approved, **with its reason**. | **→** |

## The turn

| # | Time | On screen | Say | Click |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 13 | 1:29–1:39 | Slide: "That was the brief. And what every team built." | That was the brief: evidence in, ranked requirements with reasoning, the PM decides. Honestly, **that is what every team built.** So we went back to product managers. | **→** |
| 14 | 1:39–1:54 | Slide: the quote appears word by word | A former product manager at **Vodafone** told us this. *(pause, let the audience read)* Projects run for years. **PMs change. And the "why" gets lost.** | **→** |
| 15 | 1:54–1:58 | Slide: "Six months later. A handover." | So: **six months later**, a new PM takes over. | **→** |

## Demo 2: the memory

| # | Time | On screen | Say | Click |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 16 | 1:58–2:03 | Project Diary; April activity on the calendar | Day one, the new PM opens the **Project Diary**: every decision on this car, day by day. | **Storyline** |
| 17 | 2:03–2:07 | Storyline menu | We pick **Onboarding**… | **Onboarding** |
| 18 | 2:07–2:10 | Date range filled in | …from the first decision until today. | **Generate storyline** |
| 19 | 2:10–2:18 | The written storyline, zoomed | And the project tells its own story: **what was decided, when, and why**, instead of chasing colleagues for weeks. | **→** |
| 20 | 2:18–2:26 | The new PM types 24 months, 8 people | The new PM sets **their own constraints**: 24 months, 8 people. | **→** |
| 21 | 2:26–2:29 | "Generate the requirements" | Generate again. **Nothing uploaded.** | **Generate requirements** |
| 22 | 2:29–2:40 | Seat comfort leads, tagged **Past decision** | Seat comfort leads, and it carries a tag: **past decision**. Let us look inside. | **Evidence & reasoning** |
| 23 | 2:40–2:46 | Decision Memory block, zoomed | There it is: **approved on 14 April by the previous PM**, with the reason in their own words. | **→** |
| 24 | 2:46–2:51 | Score bar, zoomed on "Past decisions" | And it is not just a note. **Past decisions count in the ranking**, right next to customers and competitors. | **→** |

## Close

| # | Time | On screen | Say | Click |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 25 | 2:51–3:00 | Close: "Vehicle projects run for years." | Vehicle projects run for years. People change. **Decisions shouldn't get lost.** We don't replace product managers. **We give them the memory of everyone who came before.** Thank you. | – |

---

### If a judge asks during Q&A

- **"Is the data real?"** The 4,365 findings, 88 customers and 9 competitor signals come from BMW's G60 files and the competitor workbook. The uploaded customer comments are labelled demo data, and the app always shows them as "Your data".
- **"Did you really speak?"** The app supports live dictation in the browser; in this recording the speech input is simulated, because it was recorded without a microphone.
- **"Why 5 points but 9 signals?"** Points are the score; signals are the sources behind it. More signals add points up to a cap, so no single source type can dominate.
- **"What does a past decision do to the score?"** An approved decision adds 5 points to that requirement for the next PM; a rejected one adds nothing and is flagged with "check whether that reason still holds".

content.text: I don't know if we should say we aren't replacing product managers as the last line. Is there like some alternative cool sick sounding last line we could say?

Agreed, it's a defensive note to end on. A last line should land your edge (memory) with a twist the audience remembers. Some options:

1. **"Your BMW already remembers your seat position. Now your project remembers why that seat exists."**
   Callbacks to the demo: the example was seat comfort, and memory seats are a real BMW feature. Clever, specific, gets a smile. **My pick.**

2. **"People change. The reasons stay."**
   Four words, very clean, easy to land with a pause.

3. **"BMW builds cars that last for years. We make sure the decisions behind them do too."**
   Ties into vehicle lifecycles, very on-brief for BMW judges.

4. **"The ultimate driving machine deserves a memory to match."**
   Plays on BMW's famous slogan. Bold, a bit cheesy, so it depends on your delivery.

5. **"Decisions outlive the people who make them. Now, so do the reasons."**
   Sounds the most "pitch-final".

A strong combo: the setup line already in the script ("Projects run for years. People change. Decisions shouldn't get lost.") followed by #1 as the punchline.

One thing to know: the closing slide in the walkthrough also shows the "We don't replace product managers…" line on screen. Tell me which line you pick and I'll update both the script and the slide. Rebuilding the slide doesn't need a new recording, so it takes seconds.
